title: A nine-year-old on the adult ward
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative and follow the module text; they are not targets. No doses are given. The pediatric protocol, the pediatric formulary and the pediatric nephrologist decide every order.
intro:
You are the internal medicine resident on a shared night call in a provincial hospital in Nueva Ecija. The pediatric ward is full, so Mark Anthony “Jun-Jun” Cruz, 9, has been admitted to the adult medical ward after three days of vomiting and watery diarrhea. He is tired and has passed little urine since morning. The hospital has no pediatric nephrologist on site.

The emergency room note reads: blood pressure 134/88 mm Hg, weight “about 30 kg per mother,” creatinine 0.9 mg/dL “normal,” sodium 131 mmol/L. The admitting order, copied from the adult template, is a hypotonic dextrose-saline solution, one liter every eight hours. His mother, Aling Marites, sits on the edge of the bed holding his hand.

n1.prompt: Which numbers do you trust, and what do you do first?

choices.text: His pressure of 134/88 is above 130/80, so it is stage 1 hypertension. Start treatment and recheck tomorrow.
choices.feedback: The adult-style cut points of the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) 2017 guideline apply from age 13. At 9, hypertension is defined by percentiles for age, sex and height, and a reading from an unknown cuff is not a diagnosis.
choices.then: You hold off. The nurse weighs and measures him and repeats the pressure with a cuff that fits his arm.

choices.text: Weigh and measure him, repeat the pressure with the right cuff, read it against percentiles.
choices.feedback: Every fluid, dose and equation in a child depends on a measured weight and height. A cuff that is too small gives a falsely high pressure, and under 13 the reference is the percentile chart, not a fixed number. The cuff bladder is at least 40% of his arm circumference; percentiles for age, sex and height.
choices.then: He weighs 26 kg and is 130 cm tall. With a correctly sized cuff his pressure is 104/66 mm Hg, within the normal range on the AAP chart for his age, sex and height.

choices.text: Repeat the pressure with the ward’s standard adult cuff and use the mother’s estimate of his weight.
choices.feedback: Repeating the pressure is right, but an adult cuff on a child’s arm gives a wrong reading, and an estimated weight carries its error into every fluid and dose you write.
choices.then: The nurse finds a pediatric cuff, weighs him and measures his height.

n2.scene: The nurse says, “His creatinine is 0.9, so his kidneys are fine.” The laboratory printout flags nothing; its reference range is for adults.
n2.prompt: How do you read 0.9 mg/dL in this boy?

choices.text: Look for an earlier creatinine from a clinic visit to compare with before deciding anything.
choices.feedback: A baseline is useful, but most healthy children have none. You can judge today’s value now, against a child’s reference and a pediatric equation.
choices.then: There is no earlier value. You enter his height and creatinine in the CKiD U25 calculator.

vitals.scr: 0.9 mg/dL: low eGFR for age (CKiD U25)

choices.text: Calculate his eGFR with the adult equation the laboratory uses, and compare it with the normal range.
choices.feedback: Adult equations do not apply to children. Creatinine-based GFR in a child depends on height, which adult equations ignore.
choices.then: You switch to the CKiD U25 calculator with his measured height.

vitals.scr: 0.9 mg/dL: low eGFR for age (CKiD U25)

choices.text: Agree that it is normal. The low urine output is from the diarrhea and will fix itself.
choices.feedback: Normal creatinine in a 9-year-old is much lower than in an adult, because it rises with age and muscle. Calling 0.9 normal hides acute kidney injury (AKI) in a child who is still losing fluid.
choices.then: The fellow on call, reviewing the admissions, asks you to recalculate with the CKiD U25 equation.

vitals.scr: 0.9 mg/dL: low eGFR for age (CKiD U25)

choices.text: High for a 9-year-old: use CKiD U25 with his height; this is AKI until proven otherwise.
choices.feedback: Creatinine comes from muscle, so a child’s normal value is much lower than an adult’s. The CKiD U25 equation uses age- and sex-specific constants and height, and gives a low estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) for his age. The Chronic Kidney Disease in Children under-25 (CKiD U25) equation with his measured height.

vitals.scr: 0.9 mg/dL: low eGFR for age (CKiD U25)

n3.prompt: What do you do with the adult fluid order?

choices.text: Leave it running. He is dehydrated and needs the volume, and he is almost an adult’s size.
choices.feedback: A fixed adult liter-rate is not scaled to his weight, and hypotonic fluid in a sick child causes hyponatremia. His sodium is already 131.
choices.then: You stop the adult order and write a weight-based plan from the pediatric protocol.

choices.text: Change to an isotonic solution but keep the adult rate of a liter every eight hours.
choices.feedback: Isotonic is right, but the volume must scale with his weight. With AKI, an adult rate risks overload in a 26-kg child.
choices.then: You recalculate the rate from his weight using the pediatric protocol.

choices.text: Stop all fluids; his kidneys are failing and fluid will overload him.
choices.feedback: He is still losing fluid from diarrhea, and the low urine output is likely from volume depletion. Withholding fluid can deepen the kidney injury.
choices.then: The nurse questions the order. You write a weight-based isotonic plan from the pediatric protocol.

choices.text: Stop the adult order; weight-based isotonic fluids per pediatric protocol, with review.
choices.feedback: The AAP 2018 guideline recommends isotonic maintenance fluids for children, but excludes kidney disorders that need an individual plan. A child with AKI falls into that group, which is why the specialist should shape the plan. Record intake and urine output, recheck sodium, and have the plan reviewed by the pediatric nephrologist.

n4.scene: The nearest pediatric nephrologist is at a regional center two hours away. It is 22:15 on a Friday.

choices.text: Call the pediatric nephrologist tonight, inform your attending, and raise transfer with the mother.
choices.feedback: Every child with AKI is an indication to call the pediatric nephrologist, by phone if none is on site. In the Philippines, transfer often depends on money and transport, so that conversation should start early. By phone or teleconsultation; begin talking with Aling Marites about what a transfer would involve.

choices.text: Call the pediatric nephrologist in the morning, at a reasonable hour, if he has not improved.
choices.feedback: A night of the wrong plan is what the call is meant to prevent. A child with AKI on an adult ward is the case the specialist wants to hear about tonight.
choices.then: Your attending, told of the admission, asks you to call the pediatric nephrologist now.

choices.text: Manage it yourself. AKI is AKI, and adult principles apply to a child his size.
choices.feedback: The errors on adult services come from adult habits: references, fluids and doses. The module asks you to change those habits and then call the pediatric nephrologist.
choices.then: The fellow reviewing admissions asks you to call the pediatric nephrologist and your attending.

n5.scene: Jun-Jun now has a fever of 38.3 °C. The nurse asks you to order paracetamol, “the usual adult tablet, half if you like.”

choices.text: Half an adult tablet is close enough for a child his size.
choices.feedback: Children’s doses are by weight or body surface area, with maximums. Guessing from an adult tablet is how dosing errors happen, and his kidneys are already injured.
choices.then: The nurse asks for a written dose. You look it up in the pediatric formulary by his weight and ask the fellow to check it.

choices.text: Use the dose you remember from your pediatric rotation, adjusted roughly for his size.
choices.feedback: Memory is where pediatric dosing errors start. Use the formulary and a second person.
choices.then: You check the pediatric formulary by weight; the fellow confirms it.

choices.text: Dose from his measured weight with the pediatric formulary, checked by a second person.
choices.feedback: A measured weight, the pediatric formulary and a second check together are the module’s safeguard against adult habits. They take five minutes. Check the maximum dose too.

end.title: Sunday
end.text: By Sunday the diarrhea has stopped, his urine output has recovered and his creatinine is falling. The pediatric nephrologist, by teleconsultation, agrees that he can stay and be followed in her clinic, with a repeat creatinine read by the pediatric equation. You explain the plan to Aling Marites, who gives permission, and to Jun-Jun in words he understands, and he agrees to the blood test.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Measure before you interpret: weight, height and a correctly sized cuff (bladder at least 40% of the arm circumference).
  • Change four things at once when a child arrives on an adult service: the creatinine reference (a pediatric equation such as CKiD U25), the blood pressure reference (percentiles under 13), the fluid plan (weight-based, isotonic, per the pediatric protocol) and the dose source (the pediatric formulary with a second check).
  • AKI in a child is a reason to call the pediatric nephrologist, by phone or teleconsultation if none is on site, and to start the transfer conversation early.
  • Parents give permission; the child gives assent as he is able.

See The child on an adult team.
